item.title: IDEA: This Italian ancient sea grotto is officially the best beach in Europe for 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Far from the crowds of the Amalfi Coast and the Cinque Terre, the little beach town of Sperlonga tempts visitors with promises of sun, sand, and a bit of ancient history to boot. Popular among Romans thanks to its proximity to the Eternal City, it has remained relatively under-the-radar among international travellers. That’s about to change, though, as Sperlonga has been voted the best beach in Europe in our 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards. I first visited Sperlonga around 15 years ago, driven by curiosity about this fabled town that my Roman friends would wax poetic about. It wasn’t until recently, though, that I fully fell under its spell. I’m not the first and certainly won’t be the last – Odysseus himself is believed to have washed up ashore nearby. Legend has it that he fell under the spell of the sorceress Circe, who likely lived on Monte Circeo, which lies a couple of towns up the coast. One of the towns that makes up the Ulysses Riviera, aptly named for Homer’s hero, Sperlonga is also a member of the Borghi Più Belli d’Italia, (Most Beautiful Villages in Italy), an association dedicated to preserving Italy’s prettiest small towns. The whitewashed historic centre sits high up on a promontory overlooking the coast, whose golden sand beaches stretch for miles, gently lapped by the azure Tyrrhenian Sea. To get up to the old town, you climb a series of stairs hewn into the side of the cliff, which lead to a warren of narrow lanes lined with shops. Once at the top, the street opens out onto a spacious piazza dotted by cafés where people gather on warm evenings for aperitivo before migrating to the restaurants serving up the catch of the day. This part of town developed during the Middle Ages, when Saracen pirate attacks pushed Sperlonga’s inhabitants to begin building on higher ground, where it was safer and they could monitor the coast. Down below, Sperlonga’s four beaches have been awarded with a Blue Flag for their cleanliness and outstanding water quality. You can bring your own umbrella and towels if you want to post up at one of the free beaches or rent lounge chairs and umbrellas at one of the many beach clubs, as my husband and I did when we visited this summer. Just be sure to book ahead if you want to have lunch at beach clubs like Bazzano Beach, where we savoured a perfect fritto misto and spaghetti with clams, washed down with a crisp local white wine. Sperlonga gets its name from the Latin word ‘speluncae,’ meaning caves or grottoes, which are abundant on this stretch of the coast. After lunch at Bazzano Beach, I climbed up the hill and walked along Via Flacca, the coastal road, to visit the Villa of Tiberius and the attached National Archaeological Museum. During the 1950s, when the road was under construction, workers discovered the ancient villa and a grotto that the Roman emperor had filled with colossal sculptures depicting characters from the Odyssey. When the local townspeople heard about the government’s plans to move the sculptures to Rome, they rose up and protested, blocking the vehicles and defending their heritage. In the end, this museum was built to house the incredible archaeological finds here. Little remains of the villa except for the foundations, but walking through the site, you can appreciate what an incredible location Tiberius chose. Archaeologists believe that he hosted lavish banquets in the grotto, entertaining his guests, who dined amid the sculptures. Gazing up at the hulking figure of Polyphemus, the cyclops, as he’s about to be blinded by Odysseus, you can imagine what an impression these marble artworks must have made. Perhaps tied to the recent release of Christopher Nolan’s film interpretation of The Odyssey, a series of street art-style murals depicting scenes from the book has been painted onto the walls of the old town. Verses from Homer’s epic poem are written along the stairs. The artist behind these works is Marco Longo, founder of Robof Studio in the neighbouring town of Terracina. These days a visit to Sperlonga doesn’t require the kind of epic journey that Odysseus undertook. On the contrary, the town is easy to reach thanks to a regional train that takes about an hour and 20 minutes from Rome, making it a convenient day trip from the city. There are no luxury resorts in Sperlonga, but should you decide to stay for a weekend, you’ll find clean, simple accommodations at Hotel La Nave, a retro family-run hotel right on the beach. Guests get complimentary access to the loungers and umbrellas at the beach club.

item.title: IDEA: 31 Thanksgiving Pies Worth a Second Slice at Breakfast
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Some people will happily eat a slice of cheesecake after Thanksgiving dinner. We respect that. But this list of Thanksgiving pie recipes is for those of us who already have our forks poised over the pie table, whipped cream at the ready. You’ll find the classics: silky pumpkin pie, gooey pecan pie, and apple pie with a double crust and another with cinnamon crumble. Then things get interesting: cranberry meringue with lime-sharpened curd, butterscotch custard with a blanket of toasted marshmallow, a pecan cream pie that doesn’t know when to stop layering. We’ve also got chilled chocolate pies, citrusy custards, and more than a few excellent candidates for breakfast the next morning. Need more inspiration? Browse our favorite pie recipes or the rest of our Thanksgiving desserts. For help with the pastry, check out our guide to making better pie or the best store-bought pie crusts.

item.title: REVIEW: 8 of the best family-friendly hotels in Lapland for a magical Arctic escape
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Find me a parent that hasn’t dreamt of one day whisking the kids off to white wilderness Finland for a stay at one of the best hotels for families in Lapland? Not only so little ones can whisper their Christmas wishlist into Santa’s ear while they still believe, but also for the chance to bring to life the Arctic of childhood dreams. Flakes falling in the forest and snow piled as high as a house. Howling huskies, hungry for the run. Reindeer and sleigh bells. Igloos that gaze up to Nordic skies as the Northern Lights erupt in a dazzling display of greens, pinks and purples. It’s the hotly Instagrammed Frozen fantasy. Getting it right matters. After all, you’re only likely to do this once. Sadly arriving by sleigh isn’t an option (yet?) but you can fly to Santa’s HQ, Rovaniemi, in three and a half hours from the UK, and flight times are now roughly the same from Gatwick to Kuusamo, with Air Baltic launching new direct flights for the 2026 winter season. Connections to other regional airports go through Helsinki. Journey aside, whether you’ve got your heart set on an igloo sculpted from snow or a glass-fronted cabin with gasp-worthy views of the aurora, a private hot tub and a storytelling elf, we’ve got you covered. Read on for our eight favourite Lapland hotels for families. Editor's picks: Best for spotting the Northern Lights: Apukka Resort How we choose the best family-friendly hotels in Lapland Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. For more information on how we review hotels and restaurants, please look at our About Us page. This is our pick of the best family-friendly hotels in Lapland. More family-friendly hotel recommendations

item.title: American reopens its most exclusive lounge offering at LAX, expands access to business class
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
After a six-year hiatus, American Airlines’ most exclusive lounge offering at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) is back in business. This week, the carrier reopened Flagship Dining at LAX. That’s American’s a la carte restaurant-style experience, which is available to customers flying in its most premium seats. It had been closed since 2020 but is now open again after a face-lift. And it also has a new access policy at LAX — and at the two other American hubs that offer the service. How to get Flagship Dining on American Airlines American now offers Flagship Dining at three of its hubs: - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) - Miami International Airport (MIA) At those airports, you'll find the a la carte dining experience is available within its Flagship Lounge, AA's premium lounge that's open to premium cabin passengers and AAdvantage elites taking long-haul flights. Instead of grabbing food at the buffet, Flagship Dining offers flyers a sit-down meal with table service — we’re talking a full menu with coursed-out dishes, all complimentary. In the past, the airline limited access to Flagship Dining to passengers flying in its Flagship First cabin on the Boeing 777-300ER or Airbus A321T aircraft. But as the carrier gets set to phase out its international-style first-class cabin, access to Flagship Dining is opening up to more passengers. In September, American began allowing passengers in its Flagship business-class cabins to sit for its exclusive dining experience. If you’re flying out of DFW, MIA or LAX, you can have a Flagship Dining meal if you are: - Booked in a Flagship Business Plus seat on the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner or Boeing 777-300ER - Booked in business-class on a qualifying long-haul, transcontinental or Hawaii flight that’s marketed as Flagship That change is especially notable at LAX, because it allows business-class passengers to use Flagship Dining on certain transcontinental flights. To get in, you'll need to have a ticket that's marketed as "Flagship" (domestic first-class tickets won't be enough). Like with any restaurant or airport lounge, space is limited. You can join the waitlist for a table after arriving at the Flagship Lounge in LA, Dallas and Miami. American used to offer Flagship Dining at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). Today, the carrier instead operates its three premium lounges (Greenwich, Chelsea and Soho) in Terminal 8 with partner British Airways. Meanwhile, its newest Flagship Lounge at Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) features a la carte dining within the main club. Speaking of American’s “Flagship” product, the end is rapidly approaching for Flagship First. Nov. 19 will mark the last date AA offers long-haul first-class as a stand-alone product on its 777s. Those jets are getting refreshed with new interiors, with the airline ditching first-class and adding the highest business-class seat count it's ever offered. American will phase out Flagship First on transcontinental service in March. Related reading:

item.title: IDEA: Why Smart Backpackers Pack a Soft Shoe for After the Trail
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
You can tell a lot about a traveler by what they wear once the hiking boots come off. Some people collapse into the same damp sneakers they wore all day. Others go barefoot in a hostel bathroom that has seen better decades. The most relaxed usually have a third option: a soft, easy shoe they put on only when the day is done. That small swap sounds trivial until you spend twelve hours on your feet. Long travel days-city museums back to back, a border crossing that eats the afternoon, a trek ending after dark-leave your feet swollen, hot, and sore in places hiking boots never reach. A dedicated after-hours shoe will not fix a bad itinerary, but it does make the evening part of the trip feel like recovery instead of more endurance. Guidebooks obsess over trailheads, bus schedules, and the best coffee near the square. Almost nobody writes about the hour between "we made it" and "I can sleep." That hour is when you cook on a hostel stove, walk to a nearby market, sit on a balcony with a beer, or stand in line for a shower that may not have hot water. It is also when much gear fails the comfort test. Trail runners and boots lock your foot in place. They are excellent for miles and terrible for lounging. Flip-flops are fine in dry heat but miserable on cold hostel floors, gravel courtyards, or anything slightly sharp. Socks alone are a hygiene gamble. You want something you can slide into without thinking, that keeps your feet warm enough for shoulder-season evenings, and lets you walk a few blocks without feeling like you left half your kit in the room. What "Recovery Footwear" Actually Means on the Road Runners have talked about recovery shoes for years. The idea is simple: after a hard effort, give your feet a different shape and a softer ride so they can settle down. Travelers get the same kind of load-just spread across airports, cobblestones, and day packs instead of track workouts. A good recovery option for backpacking usually has a few traits in common: - Easy on, easy off. You will put these on and take them off a dozen times a day. Laces that need retying every time you leave the bunk lose their charm quickly. - A footbed that does not feel like cardboard. After a long day, a little cushion and some arch support go further than another thin foam layer. - Enough coverage for cool evenings. Open slides are great in summer. In mountain towns or winter city breaks, you want something that covers more of the foot. - Light enough that you do not resent packing it. If it takes a packing cube of space, you will leave it at home and regret it later. That last point matters more than brand claims. Every item in a backpack has to earn its weight. This is where a clog-style shoe makes sense for travel, especially once the weather turns. The VALSOLE Hearth Clog is built as an indoor-outdoor recovery clog: soft molded footbed, covered upper, and a silhouette you can wear from a bunk room to a late dinner without looking as if you forgot your real shoes. We make the Hearth Clog for people who spend a lot of time on hard floors and want something kinder than a house slipper when they step outside. Backpackers live that life every day-just in hostels, trains, and rented apartments instead of a home kitchen. A few details that travel well: You can wear it with or without socks. In a heated hostel common room, barefoot works. On a cold train platform or wooden cabin floor in the mountains, a light sock plus the clog is an easy upgrade. It does not need a break-in ritual. Travel shoes that require a week of blisters before they feel right are the opposite of helpful. A recovery clog should feel usable on day one. It fills the gap between "shower shoe" and "going-out shoe." Many travelers pack flip-flops for bathrooms and end up wearing them to dinner because nothing else is clean. A covered clog handles both jobs more gracefully, especially in cooler months. We are not arguing that the Hearth Clog should replace your trail runners. It should not. Think of it as the shoe you put on when your trail runners finally get to rest. A Simple Packing Rule That Saves Sore Feet If you already pack a dedicated pair of walking shoes, consider adding a softer pair for evenings. The rule we use when people ask for a kit list is: - One pair for miles (boots or trail runners). - One pair for recovery and short evening walks. - Optional: a thin sandal or slide only if you are heading somewhere hot and wet. For warmer itineraries, that second pair can be a recovery slide. Our Recovery Slide is the open version of the same idea-quick to put on after a sweaty hike, useful around camp, and easy to rinse. For cooler trips or anyone who hates cold floors, the clog is usually the better second shoe. Either way, the point is the same: do not ask your hiking footwear to do every job on the trip. Mountain towns and overnight treks. You finish a hike, peel off wet socks, and want something warm before dinner. A clog stays by the guesthouse door and gets used constantly. For a glimpse of evenings in Himalayan guesthouses, see Dave's account of the Annapurna Sanctuary Trek. Long train or overnight bus days. Your feet swell in transit. Changing into a soft shoe at the station or even mid-journey if there is room makes the last stretch more bearable than forcing swollen feet back into laced shoes. City-heavy backpacking. Museums, metro stairs, and "just one more neighborhood" walks add up. An evening shoe turns the walk to a grocery store into recovery instead of another strain on the same hotspots. Shoulder season and winter travel. Sandals that seemed clever in July feel foolish in November. Covered recovery footwear earns its place the first time you walk across a cold bathroom floor at 6 a.m. Comfort gear pitches get dishonest when they promise a shoe will transform your trip. It will not. Good planning, pacing, and socks still matter more. A soft shoe also will not rehabilitate an injury or replace medical advice. What it can do is remove one avoidable annoyance: ending every day in footwear still trying to perform. Travel is already full of friction. Your feet do not need more of it after dark. If you can only bring one non-hiking shoe, ask where the trip spends its evenings: - Mostly warm beaches, boats, and camp showers? A recovery slide usually wins. - Hostels, mountain towns, winter cities, cabin floors? A clog is the more useful default. - Mixed climate with a real chance of cold floors? Pack the clog and leave the fashion sandals at home. Washability helps too. Anything that can handle a quick rinse in a sink and dry overnight earns more trust than delicate materials that smell like the bus after three days. If your after-hike routine already works, keep it. If you have been ending every day in damp sneakers out of habit, try giving your feet a different shoe when the miles are done. It is one of the cheaper comfort upgrades a backpack can carry. This story was published in partnership with VALSOLE.

item.title: New world's largest cruise ship begins sailings from Florida
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Royal Caribbean's newest megaship is set to make its U.S. debut this weekend. Passengers will board Legend of the Seas, the cruise line's third Icon Class vessel, at Fort Lauderdale's Port Everglades on Sunday for a pre-inaugural three-night trip to the Bahamas. The cruise line added the departure ahead of the ship's previously announced Nov. 11 inaugural voyage from the cruise hub, giving travelers an early chance to experience its newest Icon Class ship. The sailing will include a stop at Royal Caribbean's private island destination, Perfect Day at CocoCay, followed by a day at sea before returning to Fort Lauderdale on Nov. 11. At 248,633 gross tons, Legend of the Seas is the world's largest cruise ship, sharing the title with its two same-size Icon Class sisters, Icon of the Seas and Star of the Seas. The vessel can accommodate up to 7,600 passengers and approximately 2,350 crew members. Like its sister ships, Legend of the Seas features eight neighborhoods, seven pools and a lineup of family-friendly attractions, including Category 6, a six-slide water park. The ship also introduces several new experiences, including the Hollywood-themed Hollywoodland Supper Club and additional dining options in the AquaDome. Legend of the Seas debuted in Europe in summer 2026, sailing seven-night Western Mediterranean itineraries from Barcelona and Rome before crossing the Atlantic to begin its Caribbean season. Following two initial Bahamas sailings, Legend of the Seas will operate six- to eight-night itineraries from Fort Lauderdale to Western and Southern Caribbean destinations — including some places, like Aruba and Curacao, that don't normally see much action from Icon Class ships. Depending on the sailing, it'll also make port calls in Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic and Mexico. Plus, every sailing will visit Perfect Day at CocoCay. Rates for six-night trips begin around $1,000 per person, and eight-night trips begin around $1,400. However, prices differ greatly based on your chosen itinerary, room type and dates of travel. item.title: INSTRUCTION: Sticky Miso Chicken
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Miso, soy, and honey are a powerful trio, creating a savory marinade that could make just about anything sing (cod or salmon, broccoli or zucchini, tofu). Do have a keen eye on your chicken (especially if you have a drawer-style broiler at the bottom of your oven), checking it every so often to prevent a completely blackened cook. It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: My Go-To Marinade for Chicken Is 3 Ingredients. Need to make a substitution? - Heat broiler. Whisk ¼ cup honey, ¼ cup white miso, and 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a large bowl to combine. Add 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (the miso and soy sauce are plenty salty, so no need to season the chicken) and toss to coat. Arrange on wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet lined with foil and spoon any marinade remaining in bowl over. Broil chicken, turning halfway through, until cooked through and deeply charred in spots, 10–15 minutes (keep a close eye on it). Thinly slice chicken. Serve over steamed white rice, topped with thinly sliced scallions, if desired.

item.title: IDEA: A Costa Rican Beach Resort with a World-Class Coffee Program
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
In Hotels With Great Taste, we’re pulling back the curtain for a peek at the “special sauce” that hotels use to create memorable, meaningful culinary experiences for their guests. Check-in at Nekajui on Costa Rica’s verdant Papagayo Peninsula happens inside a sparsely furnished bungalow the staff call La Casita. But walk across the drive, past a massive ceiba tree hung heavy with lanterns, and all humility vanishes. The whole property sweeps out before you: an endless green lawn, pools cascading down two levels, and, finally, the serenely sparkling bay beyond. Nekajui is Ritz Carlton’s first Reserve resort in Central or South America. The Reserve’s are Ritz Carlton’s nod to the idea of complete escape, often in the far flung retreats—the Chinese Himalayas, or the Saudi Arabian desert. Now, the recently opened Nekajui allows you to unwind on the lush Costa Rican coast teeming with wildlife like capuchins, coatis, and iguanas. Hidden away at the remote property, you’ll also find a local coffee program that’s on par with the best big city cafes in the world. Sprawling over 1400 acres, Nekajui is a dreamy jungle beach resort that opened its doors on the secluded peninsula in February 2025. Each of the 107 rooms and suites peeks out onto treetop and ocean sunset views. Inside, the decor features outdoor access and carved wood motifs typical of the Guanacaste region. Many rooms also have access to patios large enough for morning yoga sessions and private plunge pools (take note: if a guest above you has one, you may see water splashing down your way). For larger parties, treetop tents and villas on the property afford even more space than standard rooms. The main campus includes rooms, restaurants, and a spa, but the property’s grounds extend: a funicular (like a tiny cable car) runs dramatically down the cliffs, past howler monkeys, to the beach with water warm as a pleasant bath and a cave to explore. Peruvian chef Diego Muñoz, whose career includes stints at world-renowned Spanish restaurants El Bulli and Mugaritz, leads the culinary program at the property’s main restaurants Puna and the tiny, six-seat chef’s counter within, Paruro. At Puna and Parura, Muñoz’s menu is filled with dishes with the layered flavors and artistic compositions that helped push Peruvian cuisine into the spotlight on a global stage. Puna has a fusion feel , sliding flavors and spices from Munoz’s international travels into Peruvian classics like a robust sudado, and zippy ceviche. Paruro, the chefs counter located inside Puna, is an East Asian experience with bites like a nori-cured tenderloin and a seabass curry. You’ll find one of Munoz’s best creations, a deboned, prawn-stuffed chicken wing, on both menus. It’s important to Muñoz that Puna uses local ingredients that are uncommon on Costa Rican menus. Fresh seafood, for example, can be a particular challenge to source, even as the overwhelming majority of Costa Rican territory is marine. Aspirations are high for the beverage program as well. Cooper’s is a moody, mysterious cocktail space with a menu full of unexpected Guanacaste ingredients. It leans into the speakeasy style, and as such, is invite-only, but don’t be intimidated—schmooze your server a bit, or ask your personal concierge to score you an invite. Inside, the menu is ambitious, dotted with some adventurous local distillates—goat cheese, cascara, mango leaf—which find their way into thrilling riffs on classics like the martini-esque Turrialba using fino sherry and the aforementioned goat cheese distillate. Elsewhere on the property, you can dine at Niri Beach Club, with an Iberian-focused menu, and the all-day Cafe Rincon which has sandwiches, bowls, and pastries. Nekajui’s commitment to on-the-ground ingredients shines brightest in its coffee program atCafé Rincon. Fabi Rojas operates the micro-roastery at Nekajui, which features always updating selections from each of Costa Rica’s seven coffee growing regions. For a country about the size of West Virginia, Costa Rica produces an impressive diversity of coffee: easy-drinking crowd pleasers in the lower elevations of the coastal west, bright acidic pops from Valle Occidental in the north, fruity, prize-winning geishas—one of which fetched over $300 per pound at auction—in the mountainous Los Santos region of the south central. And Fabi has nurtured personal relationships with farmers all over the country to ensure she has access to all of it. And while she’ll make your coffee however you want it, the move is to have it brewed in a vandola. The one piece clay carafe and pour-over cone looks like something that might date back hundreds of years, but the design actually came from Costa Rican coffee roaster and barista Minor Alfaro in 2015. Brewing in clay helps maintain aroma longer, and the valve into the base of the dripper allows more gentle oxygenation according to Alfaro. Oxygen is usually the enemy of coffee, but allowing a small amount in through the valve can sweeten the flavor. Besides brewing coffee better than my Chemex, each vandola is a handmade work of ceramic art—an apt vessel to showcase coffees grown, roasted, and brewed with exquisite care.

item.title: PROFILE: Inside one of London's oldest Indian sweet shops
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
"If you meet a loved one, you generally gift a box of mithai. It represents sweetness, family and tradition," explains Rushika Gupta. Rushika is part of the third generation of her family to join Gupta's, a beloved Indian sweet shop established in 1979. The time-tested shop was opened by her grandparents Jagdish Prasad and Chandtara Gupta on Drummond Street, London's original ‘Little India’ hidden near Euston Station. Since the 1960s, the street's independent sweet shops, veggie restaurants and grocery shops have served generations of Londoners. Gupta's has been a part of that history, specialising in making traditional Indian sweets, made from recipes passed down through generations. “I come from a family of entrepreneurs," Rushika says. "My grandpa worked incredibly hard moving over from India way back when, starting a business from scratch. So I think he really instilled that element of tradition and family and just really making sure that we remain close and just spread the love from India to the UK.” Now, Gupta's is owned and managed by Rushika's parents, Rikki and Rakhi Gupta, while Rushika and her brother, Ruchir, focus on the digital side of the business part-time. The shop is especially loved for its mithai, an Indian word for sweets. These range from jalebi (a golden, spiral-shaped sweet made from deep-fried batter drenched in fragrant sugar syrup, so adored that Jason Derulo even has a song dedicated to them), all the way to melt-in-your-mouth, fudge-like barfi and fragrant tiny balls of motichoor ladoo, which Rushika describes as “a little round orange treats” that are tasty when served hot. These sweets are especially popular when Diwali rolls around each autumn. “Mithai is a really important part of Diwali because it represents bringing people together. Whenever you're meeting a family member or a loved one, you generally gift a box of mithai”. Being part of the family business means Diwali is the busiest time of the year, but it's all part of the Gupta family experience. “My Diwali actually looks quite different to a lot of my friends,” Rushika explains. “So I'm normally helping here in the shop or serving customers or helping my parents and my brother. But after all of that hard work is done, we celebrate as a family. We get together. We definitely eat a lot of food. We play cards. We light up our house as well with diyas, which is all to do with the triumph of light over darkness. And it's just a time to get together with family.” “When it's not Diwali, my favourite treat on the menu is between three things. Soan papdi, which resembles a shortbread; it's really crunchy and a nice little brownie size. The motichoor ladoo, the little round orange treats, which are delicious when served hot, and then, of course, samosas. You cannot go wrong with samosas. I'd recommend having it with some of our tamarind chutney.” It certainly doesn't need to be Diwali to pay Gupta's a visit. The historic sweet shop has since expanded beyond Euston to Hendon, Kingsbury and their street food truck at Spitalfields Market – which has some seriously good lunch options, like pani puri, aloo papri chaat and samosa chaat.

item.title: Aman is coming to Puerto Rico, Wyndham expands its luxury footprint and other hotel news you missed
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Recently, TPG launched its inaugural State of Loyalty report, a "data-backed look at consumer loyalty, industry trends, the best loyalty program benefits and how far your points, miles and dollars go these days." Inside our comprehensive report, there are some interesting data points to look at, like which hotel loyalty points have increased or decreased in value over the year, the average points and cash price for hotels across the major loyalty brands, and our takeaways about what it all means. It's a nice deep-dive into the world of loyalty — and a great weekend read with a strong coffee in hand. Here's the other hotel news you need to know this week. Luxury brand Aman to open in Puerto Rico Aman has been on a significant expansion streak of late. Now, the luxury hotel brand has its eyes set on Puerto Rico with the announcement of Amantaru in Cabo Rojo. Though no opening date is available, we do know the hillside resort near the ocean will feature a hotel and residences, a wellness center, bars and restaurants and more in the Escencia development on the Southwestern coast. Wyndham is making a big play in the luxury hotel space with a new partnership with HotelREZ Hotels & Resorts. The partnership will bring more than 40 independent luxury hotels into Wyndham's Registry Collection Hotels Brand by early 2026. For fans of Wyndham Rewards, this means exciting (dare I say unexpected?) locations to earn and burn points, like The TownHouse Mykonos in Greece, TreeHouse Villas Koh Yao in Thailand and Galgorm Resort in Northern Ireland. Viceroy's NYC flagship is accepting reservations New York City's buzzy NoMad neighborhood, one of the best areas to stay in NYC, will soon be home to the Viceroy Park Avenue, scheduled to open in February 2027. Featuring 252 rooms and suites, the hotel will offer a new set of Tao Group bars and restaurants, a rooftop pool (rare for New York hotels) and a large set of wellness experiences, including the "Wellness Penthouse" for guests who want to relax in privacy, and a spa. Viceroy Park Avenue is now accepting reservations from Feb. 1, 2027, starting at $850 per night. A "Grand" hotel in Florida gets a new look — and a new name What's old is new again in St. Augustine, Florida, where the nearly 140-year-old Casa Monica Resort & Spa has emerged from a makeover with a new name: Grand Bohemian Casa Monica. The 137-room hotel, the first to join Marriott's Autograph Collection in 2010, now features Moroccan- and Spanish-inspired interiors, jewel tones, intricate tilework and original art. Guests can also enjoy the revamped Soltana Pool Lounge, complete with a new Moroccan-inspired bar, Mediterranean bites and cocktails made for sipping in the Florida sunshine. There are few things I like in life more than hotel merch. It's a fun way for those of us who are travel-obsessed to inject a little hotel love into our everyday lives at home. For example, my Corgi's dog bed is from The Beverly Hills Hotel and my favorite hat was a gift from the Four Seasons Resort Maldives at Landaa Giraavaru. Now, another brand I love, Raffles, has launched an online shop: The Little Shop by Raffles. Opening up just in time for the holidays (hey mom, you reading this?!), fans of the brand can now order everything from luxury linens to pajama sets and outfits, suitcases, fragrances and more. “For more than a century, Raffles has inspired a sense of discovery and an instinct for the extraordinary, Claudia Kozma Kaplan, Raffles chief brand officer, said in a statement. "The Little Shop is an invitation to bring that world home through a curated collection of distinctive pieces, created by Raffles and in collaboration with a selection of houses we deeply admire."
